bible.title: The Five Pillars
bible.summary: Every story, quest, and lore entry written for this world must pass these five checks. They are locked canon, not suggestions.
bible.body:
The setting is a near-future hybrid world, roughly twenty years ahead of today. Monsters, magic, soldiers, and modern technology all exist together and evolved together — magic was never a secret and never a recent arrival. Check everything you write against these:

1. **Coexistence, not collision.** Tech and magic are integrated. Mage units serve in armies, firearms can be enchanted, wards work alongside security cameras, creature handlers clock in next to truck drivers. Never write magic as an intrusion into a mundane world.
2. **Grounded near-future life.** Smartphones, drones, armored vehicles, magical power grids, cybernetic implants, surveillance systems. Villages lean traditional; the four major cities showcase the full magic-tech fusion.
3. **Monsters as ecology.** Creatures belong to biomes, with habitats, behaviors, and resources. They are not spawn points, and a good creature story knows where its creature lives and why.
4. **Factions reflect the fusion.** Every faction has its own relationship with magic, technology, and creatures — that relationship is usually the most interesting thing about it.
5. **Magic has a price.** Magic is rare and costly, and the temptation of infused magic and its corruption is a core moral engine. See [[the-three-origins-of-magic]] and [[the-harvest-economy]].

bible.title: The Three Origins of Magic
bible.summary: There are exactly three ways to wield magic, and extraction kills the source. This is the setting's darkest load-bearing wall — do not add a fourth origin.
bible.body:
Magic is rare, costly, and dangerous, and there are only three ways to hold it:

1. **Born with it (very rare).** Natural casters are born — scarce enough to be hunted, recruited, protected, or feared. Being born magical is a life sentence to being valuable.
2. **Infused by science.** Magic can be extracted from magical creatures or magical humans and infused into ordinary people — but extraction **kills the source**. Every dose of infused power cost a life somewhere.
3. **Gifted by magical creatures (rarest).** A very rare magical creature can willingly gift magic to a person. A gifted user's power consumed no one — see [[essence]] for why that matters.

Infusion is **temporary** — it fades and must be repeated, creating permanent demand for extraction. And every infusion **mutates the user**, slowly turning them toward an uncontrollable abomination ([[the-seven-phases-of-corruption]], [[abominations]]).

Schools of magic are extensible by design: elemental, necromancy, blood, summoning, shapeshifting, gravity, bionic/technomantic, illusion, warding, healing, spirit, shadow, time-fracture, force/kinetic, and more. Inventing a school is fair game on the board; inventing a fourth origin is not.

bible.title: The Seven Phases of Corruption
bible.summary: Corruption has seven phases, each phase is a floor you can never fully descend below, and it can be hidden but never erased. Write it as a debt, not a status effect.
bible.body:
Corruption is the price of infused power, and its arithmetic is merciless: it rises with each infusion, it alters appearance, stats, and how NPCs react — and once a person reaches a new phase, reduction can only return them to that phase's floor. Small amounts can be worked off over time. It can never be fully erased. At full corruption, the person is gone and an abomination stands where they stood.

Corruption can be *hidden* — masks, medicine, cybernetic disguise, forged medical scans, bribed doctors, social deception — but suspicion from factions and companions grows independently of the disguise. That gap between what is true and what is believed is some of the best story material in the setting.

For writers: corruption is genuinely useful short-term and damaging long-term, and both halves must stay true. A character who refuses infusion in a crisis is making a real choice with a real cost, and so is the one who doesn't. Tino's hidden tremor ([[tino]], [[the-cost-of-borrowed-power]]) is the canonical way to show it: a tell, not a lecture.

bible.title: The Taxonomy of Monsters
bible.summary: Monstrosity, abomination, demon: three words that are never interchangeable. Each generates different quests, different factions, and different guilt.
bible.body:
The setting's horrors sort into distinct categories, and the distinction carries moral weight:

- A **monstrosity** was *made* — bred or engineered in a lab, a breeding facility, a corporate program. Its existence is someone's business decision. See [[monstrosities]].
- An **abomination** was once a *person* — an infusion user who reached the end of the seven phases. Every abomination used to be someone, and somewhere there may be people who remember who. See [[abominations]].
- A **demon** is a *true supernatural being* — not a mutated human, not an engineered creature. Supernaturals are a separate force category with their own motives, hierarchies, territories, bargains, and long-term plans. See [[true-demons]] and [[the-ashen-court]].

Alongside these live natural monsters and magical creatures — the ecology of [[the-five-pillars]] — which are neither made, fallen, nor invading; they simply live here, which is exactly why [[the-harvest-economy]] hunts them.

Writers: pick the right word and the quest half-writes itself. Rescue, liberation, sabotage, or profit for a monstrosity site; grief, mercy, or cover-up for an abomination; bargain, war, or worship for the supernatural.

bible.title: The Look of the World
bible.summary: Art direction law: near-future fusion worn casually, tropical war palette for the opening chapter, first-person always, and magic damage that never looks like explosives.
bible.body:
What things look like, for anyone writing scene direction:

- **The fusion is worn casually.** Enchanted firearms, wards beside security cameras, crystal ammunition loaded from ordinary crates, a field-infusion rig maintained like any other piece of kit. Nobody in-world is amazed by magic-tech; write it with the same tone as a radio or a truck.
- **Magic leaves its own scars.** Arcane damage does not look like ordinary explosives — the prologue's battlefield is canon: strange scarring, glass bowing before it breaks, gravity forgetting itself, particles that distort. If a spell hit it, a reader should know without being told.
- **Old power, new kit.** The committed visual is the hypogriff rider: an old war-beast integrated with modern equipment, never a placeholder that could be swapped for a gunship. Apply the same fusion test to everything — the [[stormglass-quarry]] is an industrial extraction site *and* an arcane relay, in one silhouette.
- **Villages lean traditional; the four major cities are the full fusion** — including the floating metropolis. The Starting Island's spaces are tropical, commercial, and violently repurposed: burning storefronts, shredded market awnings, propaganda signage, faction colors.
- **First person, always.** Even the biggest story beats stay in the player's eyes. Scale is shown through drone feeds, map tables, reflections, windows — never an omniscient camera. Write scenes that can be *witnessed*, not filmed.
- **Mature, not performative.** Soldiers curse, panic, bleed, and behave like people who might not survive the next five minutes. Swearing is situational and character-specific — nobody is competing to be the most vulgar. Humor comes from stress and character, and it never undercuts the stakes.

bible.title: The Faction Map
bible.summary: The full political landscape: thirty-five powers, from state armies to demon nobility to the faction the players themselves may one day found. Each deserves its own bible entry eventually — claim one and write it.
bible.body:
The peninsula and its islands are contested by thirty-five powers. One-line canon for each; full entries grow from here.

**State and military:** National Defense Directorate (official state military holding the peninsula) - Peninsula Expeditionary Army (frontline command fighting for territory and supply) - Peninsula Coast Guard Authority (sea patrols, rescue, blockade) - Drone Surveillance Bureau (state/corporate surveillance of cities and roads) - Abomination Containment Authority (quarantine force that may protect people or erase evidence).

**Corporate and arcane:** Aegis Extraction Consortium (corporate extraction empire) - Helix Arcanobiotics (labs creating infused soldiers and monstrosities) - Meridian Arcane Institute (elite research university, public prestige, hidden compromises) - Iron Saints PMC (soldiers, cyborgs, and security for hire) - Cybernetic Ascendancy (transhumanists pursuing cyborg/magic integration) - Foundry Workers Union (industrial labor power).

**Magic and faith:** Concordance of Natural Casters (secretive born-magic community protecting its own) - Liberation of the Gifted (militant anti-harvest resistance) - Church of the First Gift (worshippers of creature-gifted magic) - Ossuary Covenant (necromantic order: the dead as labor, warfare, and secrets) - Crimson Choir (blood-magic cabal trading sacrifice for power) - Sanctuary of Living Beasts (creature-rescue network).

**Criminal and free:** [[stormglass-cartel]] (island smugglers, illegal sea lanes, artifacts) - Black Tithe Syndicate (black-market harvesters and magic traffickers) - Bone Market Families (old-money crime: corpse, relic, and necromancy trade) - Drifter Renegade Camps (deserters, refugees, criminals, survivors) - [[tropic-pearl-trade-house]] (wealthy island merchant families) - Free Islander League (smaller-island independence) - Wardens' Monster Hunter Guild (licensed hunters split between protection and profit).

**Regional:** Floating City Council - Skybridge Transit Authority (air lanes and floating-city access) - Verdant Marsh Clans (swamp communities with old creature pacts) - Desert Nomad Compact (caravans, survival experts, relic guides) - Mountain Holdfasts (armed mountain towns and anti-corporate militias).

**Supernatural:** [[the-ashen-court]] (demon nobility pushing incursions through battlefield rifts) - The Choir Below (subterranean intelligence steering surface politics through dreams, cults, and possession) - The Pale Embassy (supernatural diplomats offering bargains and impossible gifts at terrible hidden costs) - The Riftbound Legion (organized demonic military: summoned infantry, bone engines, corrupted artillery) - The Old Hunger (ancient predatory presence worshipped by some cults and feared even by other demons).

**And one seat left open:** the Player-Founded Faction — unlocked late in the campaign, when the players stop working for the map and start redrawing it. See [[the-long-game]].

bible.title: The Island Remembers
bible.summary: The world-state ledger for the Starting Island chapter: everything the island tracks before Commander Rook commits to Defend or Flee. Quests should read from and write to this ledger — it is what makes exploration matter.

bible.title: Both Roads Lead to Arcadia
bible.summary: Branching law: Defend and Flee are both fully playable and consequential, both converge on Port Arcadia, and consequences persist without ever forking the campaign in two.
bible.body:
The convergence contract governs every branch written for this game, starting with the first one:

- **Both branches are real.** Defend and Flee are full playable arcs with preparation, escalation, and distinct climaxes — neither is a stub, and neither is dressed up as the morally correct pick.
- **Both end in the same place.** Defend's survivors wash ashore on a storm beach; Flee's boats put in at the harbour — distinct arrival points inside the same [[port-arcadia]] region, joining the same mainland content within the first short objective.
- **Consequences persist; campaigns do not fork.** The branch changes state, dialogue, companions, survivors, resources, reputation, and opening circumstances. It does not create two separately authored mainlands. Convergence never erases what the choice cost.
- **Success is measured in who and what crosses the water** — the island itself is always lost ([[the-fall-of-the-starting-island]]). Defend changes who survives the last stand; Flee changes what the boats can carry. Write endings that honor that: the win condition is the manifest, not the map.

When writing any future branch, apply the same shape: real choice, distinct consequence, shared destination, persistent state. The ledger in [[the-island-remembers]] shows the granularity to aim for.

bible.title: The Unnamed
bible.summary: The character slots canon has reserved but not yet filled. These are the invitations: claim one on the board, name them, and they become yours.
bible.body:
Production has reserved these named-character slots on the Starting Island. Each needs a name, a face, a voice, and a want — first writer to make one live on the board owns them:

- **Kestrel command staff:** the medic, the mechanic, the quartermaster, and the scout who serve under [[the-kestrel-commander]] — plus the first optional post-Tino companion, the hardest and most important slot on this list. Whoever follows the player after Tino's empty seat has to earn it against a ghost.
- **Glasswater:** the village's civilian leaders, its clinic staff, its harbourmaster, and at least two families whose fates are visible in both branches. See [[glasswater-village]].
- **The military:** the Stormglass checkpoint leaders whose survival changes Kestrel's population, and the Fort Tempest battery officer who controls the evacuation channel's guns. See [[fort-tempest]].
- **The enemy:** the Tropic Pearl field commander running the island operation from [[pearl-beachhead]], and one morally complicated trade-house representative — the entry point for writing Pearl as people rather than uniforms.
- **The mystery:** one survivor or researcher tied to the Riftwood breach and the Essence relay. Whoever they are, they know something about [[the-riftwood-breach]] that neither faction does.

House rules: check [[what-the-player-knows-about-tino]] before giving anyone knowledge of Tino's fate, and remember [[the-look-of-the-world]] — these are exhausted, believable people in a war, not archetypes in costumes.

bible.title: The Long Game
bible.summary: Where all of this is going: the campaign's endgame is control of the peninsula, taken by any means the players choose — including founding their own faction. Write stories that can matter at that scale.
bible.body:
The long-term campaign goal is **control of the peninsula**. The players can help an existing faction take it, betray factions, unify settlements, or found their own power and compete outright — in the style of Mount & Blade. Territory is won by military might, diplomacy, settlement loyalty, economic pressure, faction deals, sabotage, liberation, betrayal, or fear.

And the game does not require its players to be heroes. Heroic, pragmatic, and genuinely dark paths are all supported — including backing extraction, running harsh settlements, betraying allies, and fielding abominations or monstrosities if the chosen path allows it. Writers should resist the urge to quietly punish evil play into unviability; the setting's judgment arrives through consequences, reputations, and the people affected, not through authorial thumb-pressure.

For the writers' room this means two things. First: island and early-mainland stories should plant seeds worth harvesting at campaign scale — a faction's grudge, a settlement's debt, a survivor's loyalty. Second: any quest consequence that shifts standing, territory sentiment, or a faction's strength is playing the long game. The [[the-faction-map]] is the board; every story moves a piece.

bible.title: The Harvest Economy
bible.summary: The setting's engine of atrocity: permanent demand for extracted magic, fed by hunting, breeding, and harvesting the born and the magical — because every dose kills its source.
bible.body:
Because infusion is temporary and extraction kills the source ([[the-three-origins-of-magic]]), the world runs a permanent, self-renewing demand for magical beings. Born casters, magic monsters, and magical creatures are hunted, captured, bred, and harvested — by corporations, states, cults, and criminal rings. Scientists cross-breed magical creatures, monsters, and sometimes humans; the results are [[monstrosities]]. The users themselves decay toward becoming [[abominations]].

Every link of the chain is a story: who hunts, who breeds, who protects, who buys, and who looks away. Black-market harvesting rings. Corporate creature farms. States stockpiling casters. Abomination outbreaks in quarantined districts. A born caster hiding in a fishing village. A companion who is worth more dead than alive to the right buyer.

And the world does not wait for the players to watch: harvesting rings operate offscreen, breeding programs expand, infused NPCs degrade over time, containment breaches release monstrosities in regions the players ignore. On the Starting Island the economy is already present in miniature — the abandoned catcher camp and its creature cages, the clinic's temporary extraction ward, and the [[stormglass-quarry]] with its Essence relay, which is a large part of why the island was worth a war.

bible.title: The Ashen Court
bible.summary: Demon nobility pushing supernatural incursions through battlefield rifts — the likeliest name behind the things that climbed out of the prologue's craters.
bible.body:
Of the five known supernatural powers ([[the-faction-map]]), the Ashen Court is the one that arrives through war: demon nobility forcing incursions through rifts torn where battle has broken the world deep enough. Where the Court has pushed through, the dead rise wrong, true demons walk, and contamination spreads against the wind.

The Starting Island bears their signature. The Strike cracked the ground and [[the-risen]] climbed out with a true demon behind them; the Riftwood Interior is scarred by an active breach; the radio warned of movement under the streets. Neither Stormglass nor Pearl understands what their war invited — which is exactly how the Court prefers it.

Open questions the writers' room owns and should spend slowly: whether the Court caused the Strike or merely used it; what nobility, hierarchy, and etiquette look like among demons; what they actually want with the island; and whether the thing that took Tino answers to them, to another power, or to nothing at all. Per [[what-the-player-knows-about-tino]], no answer to that last question may be confirmed on the board yet.

bible.title: The Peninsula
bible.summary: The primary landmass and the campaign's ultimate prize: one massive peninsula, three large islands, a scatter of small ones, and a floating metropolis above it all.
bible.body:
The world of the campaign: one **massive peninsula** as the primary landmass, roughly three large islands plus several smaller ones (the Starting Island among them), and one **massive floating island** carrying the fourth major city. Settlements come in tiers — small villages, medium towns, large cities, and four major cities: three on the mainland and islands, one floating. Villages lean traditional; the major cities are the full magic-tech fusion.

Its biomes each keep their own ecology ([[the-five-pillars]]): tropics of glass-wing manticores and vine hydras; coasts of tide wraiths and drowned soldiers; forests of antlered wardens and escaped shapeshifter experiments; mountains of thunder rocs and cave necromancer colonies; farmland of scarecrow constructs and feral infused livestock; swamps of bog revenants and old creature-pact guardians; deserts of glass wyrms and bone locust clouds; lakes of mirror eels and containment-breach hybrids; and the high-altitude reaches of gravity rays and sky leviathans. Creature names are early inspiration — writers may propose better ones — but every creature belongs somewhere.

The peninsula is where [[the-long-game]] plays out, [[port-arcadia]] is its door, and everything the players do on the Starting Island echoes across the water ahead of them.

bible.title: Stormglass Landing
bible.summary: The broken coastal battlefield where the game begins: the blast zone, the demon breach, and the first view of the war. A place already lost before the first shot the player hears.
bible.body:
A three-hundred-meter stretch of broken coastal battlefield on the island's south-west, connected to Shattermarket by road and to the western cliffs by an escape trail — deliberately left on a partially collapsed spur so the opening feels trapped without making the island linear.

This is where the cold open happens ([[the-island-is-already-lost]] arc): the squad boxed in, the Strike, the crater that gave back its dead. After the prologue passes through, the Landing remains as an aftermath site — cratered ground that should be cold and is not, wrecked emplacements, the unburied, and the first rift scarring on the island. Stories set here after the opening are archaeology in a place where the archaeology can still kill you.

See [[the-strike]], [[the-risen]], and [[the-ashen-court]] for what the Landing's craters imply.

bible.title: Shattermarket
bible.summary: The island's damaged commercial district: the grocery store, the rooftop route, the stealth alleys — a civilian shopping quarter converted into a battlefield with the shelves still stocked.
bible.body:
The market and commercial district between the Landing and Kestrel: damaged storefronts, shredded awnings, abandoned cars, military barricades, and the grocery store where Tino and the player caught their first breath of the war. The tutorial's rooftop hunter sequence, stealth drop, first weapon, and first arena all happen in its streets and on its roofs ([[the-island-is-already-lost]]).

What makes Shattermarket write well is that it is a *civilian* place wearing a war it never agreed to: evacuation notices, emergency rationing signs, blood behind a service counter, one radio still playing advertisements to nobody. The people who shopped here are now in [[glasswater-village]], at Kestrel, in the clinic — or nowhere. Stories set here are about what got left behind and who comes back for it: looters, survivors retrieving what matters, Pearl patrols, and things from the craters that have learned the streets.

Steve died on these rooftops. [[steve]]

bible.title: Glasswater Village
bible.summary: A civilian fishing community above the western inlet, caught between three armies that all claim to be protecting it. The island's conscience, and the best place on it to write ordinary people.
bible.body:
A fishing village on the island's north-west coast, above the western inlet — homes, nets, drying racks, a clinic, and a community that was never asked whether it wanted to host a war. Glasswater sits between Stormglass, Pearl, and whatever is spreading from the Riftwood, and its people are the island's moral ledger: every civilian found, evacuated, fed, or abandoned is a line in [[the-island-remembers]].

The village holds reserved character slots — civilian leaders, clinic staff, a harbourmaster, and at least two families whose outcomes stay visible in both branches ([[the-unnamed]]). Its clinic includes a temporary extraction ward, which means [[the-harvest-economy]] has a foothold even here, among the people with the least protection from it.

Stories set in Glasswater are dialogue, rescue, trust, and reputation stories: what soldiers owe civilians, what civilians will pay for safety, and who is quietly selling whom. In Flee, its people are cargo capacity on somebody's manifest. In Defend, they are the reason the walls have to hold.

bible.title: The Stormglass Quarry and Essence Relay
bible.summary: The terraced industrial cut that explains the war: stormglass extraction and an arcane relay in one site. This island is not strategic — it is *valuable*.
bible.body:
A terraced industrial site east of Kestrel: heavy machinery, communications masts, and arcane infrastructure fused into one silhouette — a working monument to [[the-look-of-the-world]]. The Quarry cuts stormglass from the island's bones, and its Essence relay ties the site into the extraction economy that feeds the world's demand for magic ([[the-harvest-economy]], [[essence]]).

This is why the Tropic Pearl Trade House hired an army: the island is not a flag, it is a deposit. Whoever holds the Quarry holds the reason the war exists, which makes it the island's natural stage for sabotage-or-repair choices — cripple the relay to deny Pearl the prize, or keep it running because Kestrel needs what it produces.

A supply road runs from the Quarry to [[pearl-beachhead]], which means the enemy's logistics and the island's secret share an address. One reserved character — a survivor or researcher tied to the Riftwood/Essence mystery ([[the-unnamed]]) — knows what the extraction here may have disturbed. See [[the-riftwood-breach]].

bible.title: Northwatch Relay
bible.summary: The high ridge radio outpost — the island's eyes and voice. Whether its dishes turn again decides how much warning anyone gets, in either branch.
bible.body:
A small, high station on the island's northern ridge — antennas, a radar pad, long sightlines over three fronts, and switchback roads that make every approach a commitment. Northwatch is a scout objective and a prize: its communications state is a tracked line in [[the-island-remembers]], and restoring or losing it changes what Kestrel knows and when.

In Defend, Northwatch is early warning for the assaults to come; in Flee, it is the difference between an evacuation that sees the attack coming and one that meets it at the docks. In both, it is a long, exposed climb held by too few people — good ground for patrol combat, recon stories, and the particular loneliness of soldiers stationed above a war they can see all of and touch none of.

Its ridge trail connects toward [[fort-tempest]]; its footpath drops toward [[glasswater-village]].

bible.title: Fort Tempest
bible.summary: The north-east coastal battery whose guns command the safest channel off the island. Whoever controls Fort Tempest decides whether the boats live.
bible.body:
A coastal artillery battery on the island's north-east shore: fortifications, gun emplacements, and a battery officer ([[the-unnamed]]) with the island's heaviest responsibility — the fort's guns control the safest evacuation channel. Its operational state is a tracked line in [[the-island-remembers]], and both branches route through what that means.

In Flee, Tempest's guns are the umbrella over [[blackreef-harbour]] — the evacuation runs under their protection or it runs naked. In Defend, the fort is a strongpoint, an artillery objective, and eventually part of the last line. Either way it is the island's clearest lesson in what a position is *for*: the fort matters exactly as much as what it protects.

Stories here are military stories — squad orders, ammunition arithmetic, the discipline of a crew that knows it fires last and leaves last, if at all.

bible.title: Blackreef Harbour
bible.summary: The protected northern harbour where the Flee branch stakes everything: fishing docks, military piers, and boats that hold less than the island needs them to.
bible.body:
The island's protected northern harbour — fishing docks and military piers together, nets and ammunition crates on the same quay. Blackreef is where the Flee branch becomes physical: evacuation logistics, boat capacity and damage ([[the-island-remembers]]), civilians staged for boarding, and the final dock defense while the engines warm.

Its connections tell its story: a coast road from [[glasswater-village]] bringing the people, an evacuation road from Kestrel bringing everyone else, and the guns of [[fort-tempest]] deciding whether any of it survives contact. Somewhere along this coast is the smuggler sea cave tied to Stormglass history — a reminder that this cartel ran these waters illegally long before it defended them officially ([[stormglass-cartel]]).

Even in Defend, Blackreef matters: boats not taken are boats denied, or boats burned, or boats held as the last resort nobody says aloud. A harbour in a doomed war is never neutral ground.

bible.title: Pearl Beachhead
bible.summary: The occupied resort estate on the south-east coast where the Tropic Pearl Trade House runs its acquisition of the island — invoiced, catered, and defended.
bible.body:
The Trade House's command foothold: an occupied resort and estate on the south-east landing, where Pearl's field commander ([[the-unnamed]]) directs the island operation from furniture the previous owners paid for. The beachhead is supplied by road from the [[stormglass-quarry]] — the prize and the invader's logistics sharing one artery — and reachable by an infiltration trail through the Riftwood for players who prefer questions asked afterward.

The location is the faction in miniature ([[tropic-pearl-trade-house]]): polished officers, hired auxiliaries, cargo manifests, exotic creatures in restraints, and violence observed from a safe veranda. It is the island's stage for infiltration or assault, for meeting the named antagonist, and for the morally complicated trade-house representative — the writer's door into Pearl as people with reasons, ledgers, and limits.

What the beachhead knows and does not know about [[the-riftwood-breach]] next door is one of the island's better unanswered questions.

bible.title: The Riftwood Interior
bible.summary: The tropical interior scarred by the supernatural breach: the island's wound, its deepest mystery, and the one place on it that belongs to neither army.
bible.body:
The island's forested heart — six hundred meters of dense tropical interior that the war went around, because something else got there first. The Riftwood is scarred by an active supernatural breach ([[the-riftwood-breach]]): rift-touched ground, creatures that answer to no faction, and contamination that moves against the wind. It interrupts the island's center-east shortcut, so every trail through it is a wager — three foot-trails connect it toward Kestrel, the Quarry ravine, Northwatch, and the Pearl side, and none of them are safe.

This is the island's stage for optional exploration, creature encounters, and corruption-and-harvest storytelling: the abandoned catcher camp with its empty creature cages sits at its edge, and whatever the Quarry's extraction disturbed, the Riftwood is where it surfaces. The reserved researcher character ([[the-unnamed]]) is tied to this place.

Writers' discipline for the Riftwood: it obeys [[something-under-the-war]] — reveal in glimpses, never in briefings, and every answer should uncover two better questions.

bible.title: Monstrosities
bible.summary: Engineered horrors — cross-bred from magical creatures, monsters, and sometimes humans in labs and breeding programs. Every one of them is somebody's product.
bible.body:
A monstrosity was *made*. Corporate and state programs cross-breed magical creatures, monsters, and sometimes humans in pursuit of weapons, workers, and harvestable stock; the results that survive are monstrosities ([[the-taxonomy-of-monsters]], [[the-harvest-economy]]).

They carry a different story weight than the fallen or the supernatural: a monstrosity implies a facility, a program, a budget line, and people who signed off. Breeding sites, labs, and containment stations are natural dungeon and quest locations, with rescue, liberation, sabotage, or profit as the standing player choices — and a containment breach is a disaster with a return address.

On the Starting Island their presence is peripheral but real: corporate-bred jungle stock among the tropics' creatures, the catcher camp's cages at the Riftwood's edge, and whatever Pearl keeps in restraints at the beachhead. Writers: when a monstrosity appears, the interesting question is rarely the creature. It is the invoice.

bible.title: Abominations
bible.summary: The end of the seven phases: infusion users whose corruption completed. Every abomination used to be someone — and writing them well means never forgetting it.
bible.body:
An abomination was once a *person* — an infused user who reached the end of [[the-seven-phases-of-corruption]]. The mutation completes, control ends, and what remains is an uncontrollable creature wearing the ruin of a human life ([[the-taxonomy-of-monsters]]).

Their story weight is grief. Somewhere behind every abomination is a name, a unit, a family, possibly a companion who watched the phases advance and said nothing. Abomination outbreaks quarantine districts; the Abomination Containment Authority ([[the-faction-map]]) exists to respond to them — and to decide, case by case, whether it is protecting people or erasing evidence. Battlefield abominations already walk the Starting Island's fronts, and the clinic's extraction ward in [[glasswater-village]] is a reminder of how the pipeline starts.

The standing horror of the setting is that the player can walk this road too — corruption is a live gameplay system, not scenery. And the standing dread the writers' room must protect: Tino is an infuser, his tremor is canon, and the question of how far along he is belongs to [[what-the-player-knows-about-tino]].

bible.title: Essence
bible.summary: Extracted magic itself — the refined product of the harvest economy, drawn from sources that do not survive the drawing. The commodity the whole dark market runs on.
bible.body:
Essence is magic made portable: extracted from magical creatures and magical humans, refined, and sold into the permanent demand created by infusion's fading ([[the-three-origins-of-magic]]). Extraction kills the source — so every unit of Essence is a life converted into product, and everyone who trades it knows.

It is the fuel of the [[the-harvest-economy]]: corporations farm creatures for it, states stockpile casters against future need, black-market rings traffic it, and field-infusion rigs like Tino's ([[field-infusion-rig]]) burn it dose by dose. A gifted user's magic is remarkable precisely because it consumed no Essence at all — their power cost no one anything, which in this world is nearly a miracle.

The Starting Island produces it: the [[stormglass-quarry]] runs an Essence relay, which is a large part of why the Trade House considered the island worth a war. What relationship Essence has to stormglass itself — whether the crystal stores it, conducts it, or is something stranger — is an open lore question with a long fuse. See [[stormglass]].

bible.title: The Riftwood Breach
bible.summary: The supernatural rupture in the island's interior — older than the current battle, wider than either faction knows, and the reason the island's center belongs to no army.
bible.body:
Before the Strike cracked the Landing's craters open, something had already torn through in the island's interior. The Riftwood breach is the island's standing wound: rift-scarred ground where creatures cross, contamination drifts against the wind, and the war's two armies both quietly route around a forest neither can hold ([[riftwood-interior]]).

What opened it is unwritten — candidates include the Quarry's extraction cutting too deep ([[stormglass-quarry]]), the Ashen Court forcing a door ([[the-ashen-court]]), or something older that was always going to wake. What it implies is written: the breach predates the invasion, which means the supernatural presence on this island is not a side effect of the battle. The battle may be a side effect of *it*.

The reserved researcher character ([[the-unnamed]]) holds a piece of this. The trail of the thing that took Tino ran east, toward breach-scarred country. Per [[what-the-player-knows-about-tino]] and [[something-under-the-war]], connect those dots slowly, in glimpses, or not at all.
